messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ravi had grown up in a South Asian household where his father’s temper was unpredictable and punishment was physical, so that the sound of a door slamming in the next room, or the sting of cold air on his skin, could still feel instantly dangerous to him. At 36, married and working as a detective, he could function for long stretches, but the old fear would arrive with a bodily force that surprised him. He described being caught off guard one winter evening while stepping out of his car at the station: the metal door had swung shut hard behind him, the noise echoing in the garage, and the sharp cold on his wrists had brought him back to the helplessness of childhood. In the hours afterward he found himself thinking, with a familiar wave of shame, that his reactions since all of this showed he was a lousy coper, and that there must be something wrong with him as a person. What unsettled him most was not only the intensity of the reaction, but the way it made him feel split from himself, as though he did not know himself anymore.

Over time, these moments became the lens through which he judged his entire life. A night when his wife was away and he had to sleep alone in the master bedroom left him staring at the ceiling until nearly dawn, convinced that if he drifted off in an unfamiliar or empty house he would lose his guard and something would happen. The more these episodes seemed to expose him, the more he believed that there was something fundamentally defective in him, and that he was failing at being the sort of man, husband, and detective he had always assumed he should be. That appraisal did not stay abstract: it pushed him to avoid other people whenever he could, to turn down invitations, to keep conversations at work brief, and to find excuses not to go out after hours. He would say he was tired or busy, but privately he felt safer with distance, because being around others made him fear that they might notice how shaken and unlike himself he had become.

Yet the same habits that gave him momentary relief also fed the very fears he was trying to outrun. By staying up until very late, he could postpone the vulnerable moment of sleep, especially if he was alone, but the next day he was more drained and more on edge, and that fatigue made him even quicker to judge himself as a lousy coper. The longer he isolated himself, the less familiar his own responses felt, and the more convinced he became that something was wrong with him at his core. When he finally did go out, even something ordinary like walking from the parking lot into a store could feel loaded: a sudden door banging behind him, or cold wind striking his hands, would jolt him back into that same old certainty that he was not handling things properly and could not trust himself to stay composed. In that state he began reading every reaction as proof of damage, and each fresh surge of shame made the next retreat feel necessary.

At work, Ravi tried to preserve the image of control, but the pattern was narrowing his life. He was avoiding people more than he admitted, arranging his schedule to reduce time with colleagues, and declining social plans with his wife until she started noticing how often he was absent even when he was home. He hated how much effort it took to keep ordinary life at a distance, yet he also feared that if he stopped avoiding, he would be exposed as weak and broken. By the time he sought help, the strain had built into a quiet crisis: he was exhausted from delaying sleep, increasingly cut off from others, and frightened by how quickly a slammed door or a certain temperature against his skin could bring back the same judgments about himself. What brought him in was the fear that he was losing not only sleep, but his sense of who he was, and what he was most hoping for was a way to feel like himself again without having to keep backing away from everyone and everything around him.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers leading to distress and shame, but it does not clearly state that the reminders themselves drive the specific negative appraisals about being defective or a lousy coper within the same paragraph.
The vignette shows negative appraisals leading to avoidance, but it does not clearly describe those appraisals as increasing or generating the triggering reminders/cues themselves in any paragraph.
